## Neighbouring sites share what a model misses

[Independence of observations](independence-of-observations.qmd) found that visits to
one site repeat each other, and that resampling or splitting by site deals with it.
Sites are not independent of each other either. Two sites a few kilometres apart share
a water mass, a current and a stretch of seabed, and whatever a model's inputs miss
there, both sites miss it too.

That matters when a model is scored. Cross-validation by site holds out scattered
sites, so most held-out sites still have a neighbour among the sites the model was
fitted to. A model can then predict a held-out site well by knowing its neighbourhood,
without having learnt anything that would carry to an area nobody has surveyed. This
page shows how much of a score that can be, and how to measure what a model knows
without the neighbours.

{{< include ../../_snippets/simulated-data.qmd >}}

{{< include ../../_snippets/python-tabs-run.qmd >}}

## Spatial blocks hold out whole areas of the map

**Spatial blocks** cut the map into squares and hold out every site in a square
together. A held-out site's neighbours in the same square are held out with it, so
fewer fitted sites lie around it and its position gives less away. Cross-validation by
blocks deals the squares into folds as cross-validation by site deals out sites, and
scores the model on each fold in turn.

::: {.diagram}
![Cross-validation by site holds out scattered sites, each with fitted sites close by. Spatial blocks cut the map into squares and hold out every site in a square, so a held-out site's neighbours are held out with it and its nearest fitted site is further away. Blocks test what a model knows about areas it has not seen.](img/spatial-blocks.svg){fig-alt="Two cards showing the same map of 44 sites. Cross-validation by site, hold out scattered sites: seven held-out sites are scattered across the map, each joined by a short dashed line to the nearest site used for fitting, so a held-out site's position alone says a lot about it. Spatial blocks, hold out whole areas: the map is cut into six squares and every site in the top middle square is held out; their neighbours are held out with them and their dashed lines to the nearest fitted site are longer, so position says less about them. A note says blocks test what a model knows about areas it has not seen."}
:::

## Worked example

The data, the split by site and the negative binomial model are those of
[Distributional assumptions](distributional-assumptions.qmd). Each training site is
also given a **block**: the square of half a degree, about 40 by 55 km, that holds the
centre of its stations. Ten-fold cross-validation by site and by block, each repeated
three times with different folds, scores the models below.

### Preparing the data

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: prepare
survey <- load_coastal_survey_clean()

split <- group_initial_split(survey, group = site_id, prop = 0.75)
train <- training(split) |>
  # the half-degree square holding the centre of each site's stations
  mutate(block = paste(floor(mean(longitude) / 0.5),
                       floor(mean(latitude) / 0.5)),
         .by = site_id)

by_site <- group_vfold_cv(train, group = site_id, v = 10, repeats = 3)
by_block <- group_vfold_cv(train, group = block, v = 10, repeats = 3)

curve_recipe <- recipe(
  abundance ~ depth_m + temperature_c + chlorophyll_mg_m3 + salinity_psu +
    substrate + season,
  data = train
) |>
  step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()) |>
  step_relevel(substrate, ref_level = "sand") |>
  step_poly(depth_m, temperature_c, degree = 2, options = list(raw = TRUE))

prepared <- bake(prep(curve_recipe), new_data = NULL)
nb_fit <- MASS::glm.nb(abundance ~ ., data = prepared)
```

## Python

```{python}
import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import statsmodels.api as sm
from sklearn.compose import ColumnTransformer
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestRegressor
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer
from sklearn.metrics import root_mean_squared_error
from sklearn.model_selection import GroupKFold, GroupShuffleSplit
from sklearn.pipeline import Pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import OneHotEncoder, PolynomialFeatures

from mlbasic_data import load_coastal_survey_clean

survey = load_coastal_survey_clean()

grouper = GroupShuffleSplit(n_splits=1, train_size=0.75, random_state=123)
train_rows, test_rows = next(grouper.split(survey,
                                           groups=survey["site_id"]))
train = survey.iloc[train_rows].reset_index(drop=True)

# the half-degree square holding the centre of each site's stations
centre = train.groupby("site_id")[["longitude", "latitude"]].transform("mean")
train["block"] = (np.floor(centre["longitude"] / 0.5).astype(int).astype(str)
                  + " "
                  + np.floor(centre["latitude"] / 0.5).astype(int).astype(str))

def folds(groups):
    return [fold for r in range(3)
            for fold in GroupKFold(n_splits=10, shuffle=True, random_state=r)
            .split(train, groups=groups)]

by_site = folds(train["site_id"])
by_block = folds(train["block"])

categorical = ["substrate", "season"]
predictors = ["depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3",
              "salinity_psu"] + categorical

def squared(column):
    return (column, Pipeline([
        ("impute", SimpleImputer(strategy="median")),
        ("poly", PolynomialFeatures(degree=2, include_bias=False)),
    ]), [column])

curve_recipe = ColumnTransformer([
    squared("depth_m"),
    squared("temperature_c"),
    ("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"),
     ["chlorophyll_mg_m3", "salinity_psu"]),
    ("categorical",
     OneHotEncoder(drop=["sand", "spring"], sparse_output=False),
     categorical),
])

fitted_recipe = curve_recipe.fit(train[predictors])
design = sm.add_constant(pd.DataFrame(
    fitted_recipe.transform(train[predictors]),
    columns=fitted_recipe.get_feature_names_out()))
nb_fit = sm.NegativeBinomial(train["abundance"], design).fit(
    method="newton", disp=0)
```

:::

The `r n_distinct(train$site_id)` training sites fall into
`r n_distinct(train$block)` blocks.

### The negative binomial model's errors form patches on the map

For each training site, the animals caught over all its visits are divided by the
number the negative binomial model predicted for those visits. A ratio of 2 means the
site gave twice what its depth, temperature, seabed and the rest led the model to
expect; a ratio of ½ means half.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: site-errors
site_error <- train |>
  mutate(predicted = fitted(nb_fit)) |>
  summarise(longitude = mean(longitude), latitude = mean(latitude),
            caught = sum(abundance), predicted = sum(predicted),
            .by = site_id) |>
  mutate(ratio = caught / predicted)
```

## Python

```{python}
train["predicted"] = nb_fit.predict(design)
site_error = train.groupby("site_id").agg(
    longitude=("longitude", "mean"), latitude=("latitude", "mean"),
    caught=("abundance", "sum"), predicted=("predicted", "sum"))
site_error["ratio"] = site_error["caught"] / site_error["predicted"]
```

:::

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-errors
#| fig-cap: "Each training site's catch divided by the catch the negative binomial model predicted for its visits. Vermilion sites gave more than predicted, blue sites less. Each site's ratio is noisy, but sites of one colour gather in patches: more than predicted along the western edge, less through the middle."
#| fig-alt: !expr 'glue::glue("A map with longitude from 140 to 142.5 degrees on the horizontal axis and latitude from 41 to 43 degrees on the vertical, showing {nrow(site_error)} training sites as points coloured on a scale from blue, a quarter of the predicted catch, through grey, as predicted, to vermilion, four times the predicted catch. Colours are mixed across the map, but vermilion points gather along the western edge between about 42 and 43 degrees north, and blue points gather in the middle of the map around 141 to 141.7 degrees east and 42 to 42.3 degrees north.")'
#| fig-width: 6.5
#| fig-height: 5
ggplot(site_error, aes(longitude, latitude, colour = ratio)) +
  geom_point(size = 3) +
  scale_colour_gradient2(
    transform = "log2", midpoint = 1, limits = c(1 / 4, 4),
    oob = \(x, range) scales::squish(x, range, only.finite = FALSE),
    breaks = c(1 / 4, 1 / 2, 1, 2, 4), labels = c("¼", "½", "1", "2", "4"),
    low = ml_palette[["blue"]], mid = "grey88",
    high = ml_palette[["vermilion"]]
  ) +
  coord_quickmap() +
  labs(x = "Longitude", y = "Latitude",
       colour = "Caught ÷\npredicted")
```

:::

Each site's ratio rests on a handful of noisy counts, so the map is speckled. Even so,
@fig-errors shows patches: sites along the western edge gave more than the model
predicted, and sites through the middle gave less. Errors that gather by area mean
the model is missing something that neighbouring sites share.

The survey is simulated, so the cause is known. The simulation added a smooth pattern
over the map that no input measures: some areas hold more of the species than their
depth, temperature and seabed explain, and others less.
[Linearity and nonlinearity](linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd) found the same pattern
bending the GAM's depth curve. In real data, a patch of errors is a pointer to a
missing input, such as a front, a sediment type or a fishing closure, and is worth
explaining before it is treated as noise.

### Position alone predicts new sites from their neighbours

A model given only a station's longitude and latitude can predict a new site only by
what the sites around it caught. The negative binomial model's straight lines cannot
carve the map into patches, but the random forest of
[Forests and boosting](../03-supervised-learning/forests-and-boosting.qmd) can. Three
forests are scored, one on position, one on the environmental inputs, and one on
both, under cross-validation by site and by block.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: forest-scores
input_sets <- list(
  "Position" = c("longitude", "latitude"),
  "Environment" = c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3",
                    "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season"),
  "Both" = c("depth_m", "temperature_c", "chlorophyll_mg_m3",
             "salinity_psu", "substrate", "season", "longitude", "latitude")
)

forest_on <- \(columns) {
  workflow(
    recipe(reformulate(columns, "abundance"), data = train) |>
      step_impute_median(all_numeric_predictors()),
    rand_forest(trees = 500) |>
      set_engine("ranger") |>
      set_mode("regression")
  )
}

schemes <- list("by site" = by_site, "by block" = by_block)

forest_scores <- expand_grid(inputs = names(input_sets),
                             scheme = names(schemes)) |>
  mutate(score = map2(inputs, scheme, \(i, s) {
    fit_resamples(forest_on(input_sets[[i]]), schemes[[s]],
                  metrics = metric_set(rsq, rmse)) |>
      collect_metrics()
  })) |>
  unnest(score) |>
  mutate(.metric = if_else(.metric == "rsq", "R²", "RMSE"))

forest_scores |>
  pivot_wider(id_cols = inputs, names_from = c(.metric, scheme),
              names_sep = " ", values_from = mean) |>
  select(inputs, starts_with("R²"), starts_with("RMSE")) |>
  mutate(across(starts_with("R²"), \(x) round(x, 3)),
         across(starts_with("RMSE"), \(x) round(x, 2)))
```

## Python

```{python}
input_sets = {
    "Position": ["longitude", "latitude"],
    "Environment": predictors,
    "Both": predictors + ["longitude", "latitude"],
}

def forest_on(columns):
    numeric = [c for c in columns if c not in categorical]
    steps = [("numeric", SimpleImputer(strategy="median"), numeric)]
    if any(c in categorical for c in columns):
        steps.append(("categorical", OneHotEncoder(handle_unknown="ignore"),
                      [c for c in columns if c in categorical]))
    return Pipeline([
        ("recipe", ColumnTransformer(steps)),
        ("model", RandomForestRegressor(n_estimators=500, random_state=1,
                                        n_jobs=-1)),
    ])

def score(columns, splits):
    rows = []
    for fit_rows, held_rows in splits:
        fitted = forest_on(columns).fit(train.loc[fit_rows, columns],
                                        train.loc[fit_rows, "abundance"])
        predicted = fitted.predict(train.loc[held_rows, columns])
        truth = train.loc[held_rows, "abundance"]
        rows.append({"R²": np.corrcoef(predicted, truth)[0, 1] ** 2,
                     "RMSE": root_mean_squared_error(truth, predicted)})
    return pd.DataFrame(rows).mean()

schemes = {"by site": by_site, "by block": by_block}
forest_scores = pd.DataFrame({
    name: pd.concat({scheme: score(columns, splits)
                     for scheme, splits in schemes.items()})
    for name, columns in input_sets.items()
}).T
forest_scores.columns = [f"{m} {s}" for s, m in forest_scores.columns]
forest_scores = forest_scores[["R² by site", "R² by block",
                               "RMSE by site", "RMSE by block"]]
forest_scores.round(3).reset_index(names="inputs")
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: score-numbers
#| include: false
r2 <- forest_scores |>
  filter(.metric == "R²") |>
  select(inputs, scheme, mean) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = scheme, values_from = mean)
r2_of <- \(i, s) r2[[s]][r2$inputs == i]
three <- \(x) format(round(x, 3), nsmall = 3)
gain_site <- r2_of("Both", "by site") - r2_of("Environment", "by site")
gain_block <- r2_of("Both", "by block") - r2_of("Environment", "by block")
rmse_lower <- forest_scores |>
  filter(.metric == "RMSE") |>
  select(inputs, scheme, mean) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = scheme, values_from = mean) |>
  summarise(all(`by block` < `by site`)) |>
  pull()
```

The forest on position alone reaches an R² of
`r three(r2_of("Position", "by site"))` under cross-validation by site. It knows
nothing about the species' surroundings, only which sites lie nearby, so this score is
evidence that neighbouring sites share their catch. Under blocks it falls to
`r three(r2_of("Position", "by block"))`, because a held-out site's neighbours now
mostly sit in the same held-out block.

The forest on the environment falls too, from
`r three(r2_of("Environment", "by site"))` to
`r three(r2_of("Environment", "by block"))`. Depth follows position, as
[Linearity and nonlinearity](linearity-and-nonlinearity.qmd) found, so part of what
looked like knowledge of depth was knowledge of the area. A block also tends to hold
conditions that the rest of the map covers thinly, which
[Sampling and extrapolation](sampling-and-extrapolation.qmd) takes up.

Adding position to the environmental inputs raises R² by `r three(gain_site)` under
cross-validation by site, but by only `r three(gain_block)` under blocks. About
`r round(100 * (1 - gain_block / gain_site), -1)`% of what coordinates seemed to add
was knowledge of the neighbours, which an unsurveyed area would not have.

`r if (rmse_lower) "Every RMSE is lower under blocks, although every R² is lower too." else "The RMSEs do not move with the R²s."`
The blocks' folds hold different mixes of rich and poor sites from the sites' folds, so
their RMSEs are on different scales, the trap
[Information leakage](../02-marine-data/information-leakage.qmd) met when it compared
a random split with a split by site. R², which measures each fold against its own
spread, can be compared across the two schemes.

### Blocks leave fewer fitted sites nearby

A forest predicts a held-out site from the fitted sites around it, so the difference
between the two schemes is how many fitted sites are left near each held-out site. For
each held-out site in the first round of ten folds, the fitted sites within 30 km are
counted, measuring between the centres of the sites' stations at about 83 km to a
degree of longitude and 111 km to a degree of latitude.

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: nearby
centres <- train |>
  summarise(x = mean(longitude) * 83, y = mean(latitude) * 111,
            .by = site_id)

fitted_nearby <- \(folds) {
  folds |>
    filter(id == "Repeat1") |>
    pull(splits) |>
    map(\(s) {
      held <- filter(centres, site_id %in% assessment(s)$site_id)
      fitted <- filter(centres, site_id %in% analysis(s)$site_id)
      km <- sqrt(outer(held$x, fitted$x, "-")^2 +
                 outer(held$y, fitted$y, "-")^2)
      tibble(site_id = held$site_id, nearby = rowSums(km < 30))
    }) |>
    list_rbind()
}

nearby <- bind_rows(
  fitted_nearby(by_site) |> mutate(scheme = "By site"),
  fitted_nearby(by_block) |> mutate(scheme = "By block")
)
nearby |> summarise(median_nearby = median(nearby), .by = scheme)
```

## Python

```{python}
centres = train.groupby("site_id").agg(x=("longitude", "mean"),
                                       y=("latitude", "mean"))
centres["x"] *= 83
centres["y"] *= 111

def fitted_nearby(splits):
    nearby = []
    for fit_rows, held_rows in splits[:10]:
        held = centres.loc[train.loc[held_rows, "site_id"].unique()]
        fitted = centres.loc[train.loc[fit_rows, "site_id"].unique()]
        km = np.hypot(
            held["x"].to_numpy()[:, None] - fitted["x"].to_numpy(),
            held["y"].to_numpy()[:, None] - fitted["y"].to_numpy())
        nearby.extend((km < 30).sum(axis=1))
    return np.median(nearby)

pd.DataFrame({"scheme": ["By site", "By block"],
              "median_nearby": [fitted_nearby(by_site),
                                fitted_nearby(by_block)]})
```

:::

```{r}
#| label: nearby-numbers
#| include: false
median_nearby <- nearby |>
  summarise(n = median(nearby), .by = scheme) |>
  deframe()
none_nearby <- nearby |>
  summarise(n = mean(nearby == 0), .by = scheme) |>
  deframe()
```

::: {.panel-tabset group="language"}

## R

```{r}
#| label: fig-nearby
#| fig-cap: "Number of fitted sites within 30 km of each held-out site, in the first round of ten folds. Under cross-validation by site most held-out sites keep several fitted neighbours; under blocks most keep one or two, and some none."
#| fig-alt: !expr 'glue::glue("Two bar charts, one above the other, counting held-out sites by how many fitted sites lie within 30 km of them. By site: the bars spread widely, with a median of {median_nearby[[\"By site\"]]} fitted sites. By block: the bars pile up at the left, with a median of {median_nearby[[\"By block\"]]} and a tall bar at none.")'
#| fig-width: 7
#| fig-height: 4.4
nearby |>
  mutate(scheme = fct_relevel(scheme, "By site")) |>
  ggplot(aes(nearby)) +
  geom_bar(fill = ml_palette[["blue"]]) +
  facet_wrap(~scheme, ncol = 1) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = 0:12) +
  labs(x = "Fitted sites within 30 km", y = "Held-out sites")
```

:::

@fig-nearby shows the difference. Under cross-validation by site, a held-out site
typically keeps `r median_nearby[["By site"]]` fitted sites within 30 km. Under blocks
it typically keeps `r median_nearby[["By block"]]`, and
`r round(100 * none_nearby[["By block"]])`% of held-out sites keep none at all. The blocks
do not remove every neighbour: a site near the edge of its block can still sit close to
fitted sites across the line. How large to make the blocks is a choice of its own,
which [Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd)
makes.

## Each resampling scheme answers its own question

Neither score is the right one in general. Cross-validation by site measures how well a
model predicts a new site among those already surveyed, such as an unsampled site
between two monitored ones. Blocks measure how well it predicts an area nobody has
surveyed, which is what a habitat map of a new region needs. Report the scheme that
matches the use, and say which it was.

## Time adds a direction to the same problem

Samples close in time resemble each other as samples close in space do: one year's
cold winter, or one month's bloom, touches every station sampled then. The same
remedy applies, with one difference.

| | In space | In time |
| --- | --- | --- |
| What is shared | Neighbouring sites' water and seabed | A season's or a year's conditions |
| What a split by site leaks | The neighbourhood | The future, when later years train the model |
| The honest split | Hold out whole areas | Fit to earlier years, test on later ones |

Predicting 2021 from a model fitted to 2022 is not merely optimistic; it can never
happen in use. A forecast is scored only by holding out the years after the ones the
model was fitted to.
[Spatial and temporal cross-validation](../07-validation/spatial-and-temporal-cv.qmd)
builds both kinds of split.

## Key points

::: {.key-points}
- Neighbouring sites share water and seabed, so a model's errors gather in patches on
  the map. A patch points to something the inputs miss.
- Cross-validation by site leaves most held-out sites with a fitted neighbour close by,
  so a model can score well by knowing the area.
- A random forest on longitude and latitude alone scored an R² of
  `r three(r2_of("Position", "by site"))` by site and
  `r three(r2_of("Position", "by block"))` by block. Adding position to the
  environment looked worth `r three(gain_site)` by site and `r three(gain_block)` by
  block.
- **Spatial blocks** hold out whole areas and measure what a model knows about places
  nobody surveyed. Choose the scheme that matches the model's use.
- Compare R², not RMSE, across resampling schemes. In time, test only on years after
  those the model was fitted to.
:::

## Try it yourself

1. Change the blocks from half a degree to a quarter, `/ 0.25` in both places, and
   rerun. Predict first whether the forest on position should score higher or lower
   under the smaller blocks, then count the fitted sites nearby again.
2. Score the forest on position with `vfold_cv(train, v = 10)`, which deals single
   stations into folds and so lets a site's other visits train the model. How much
   higher does position score when a held-out station's own site is in the training
   data?
